docs.text: • Authorization · Observability · Web Security

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: Packages: Asdamir.Core (JWT, encryption, contracts), Asdamir.Web (Blazor auth state, token propagation)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Asdamir authenticates users with JSON Web Tokens (JWT) and supports refresh-token rotation and two-factor authentication (2FA). The building blocks live in Asdamir.Core; the Blazor-side auth state and bearer-token propagation live in Asdamir.Web.

docs.title: JWT issuance & validation
docs.text:
IJwtService (Asdamir.Core.Contracts) issues access tokens and reads claims. Configure it from the Jwt section:

// appsettings.json — non-secret defaults; Jwt:Key comes from secrets
"Jwt": {
  "Issuer":   "asdamir-adminconsole-api",
  "Audience": "asdamir-adminconsole-clients",
  "AccessTokenLifetimeMinutes": 15,   // fallback; see DB-driven lifetimes below
  "RefreshTokenLifetimeDays": 14
}

DB-driven, per-app lifetimes. When AppManagement issues a token for a managed app (app-login/app-refresh, below) it reads the lifetime from that app's dbo.AppConfigurations (Jwt:AccessTokenLifetimeMinutes / Jwt:RefreshTokenLifetimeDays, AppId-scoped) and passes it to the explicit-lifetime IssueTokens(user, perms, accessLifetime, refreshLifetime) overload. It is re-read on every login/refresh, so changing it in the DB takes effect without a redeploy. The Jwt:* config above is only the fallback. See Configuration.

// Jwt:Key (>= 64 bytes) is supplied via user-secrets / environment, never appsettings.
public sealed class LoginHandler(IJwtService jwt)
{
    public TokenResult Issue(UserAuth user) => jwt.IssueTokens(user);
}

Issuer/Audience must match between the issuing service and every validator. Keep them identical across the API and any client that validates the token.

docs.title: Signing keys: symmetric or asymmetric
docs.text:
JwtKeyMaterial.FromConfiguration (Asdamir.Core.Services) resolves what a host signs with and what it accepts, from the Jwt section. Which settings are present decides the shape:

Setting Host role Signs Validates Jwt:SigningKeyPem (EC P-256 private key) the issuer ES256, with a kid ES256 Jwt:PublicKeyPem (the issuer's public key) a validator nothing — it cannot mint a token ES256 Jwt:JwksUrl (the issuer's key-set URL, https) a validator that follows key rotations nothing ES256, with keys fetched from the issuer Jwt:Key alone (≥ 32 bytes) issues and validates its own tokens HS256 HS256

Use the asymmetric pair whenever the host that validates a token is not the host that issued it: a symmetric key shared between hosts lets every holder mint any token, including one for a more privileged audience. Jwt:Key alone stays correct for a self-contained app that issues and validates its own tokens.

var keys = JwtKeyMaterial.FromConfiguration(builder.Configuration);
builder.Services.AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer(o =>
{
    o.TokenValidationParameters = new TokenValidationParameters
    {
        ValidIssuer = issuer, ValidAudience = audience, ValidateLifetime = true,
    };
    keys.ApplyTo(o.TokenValidationParameters);   // keys + the pinned algorithm list
});
  • ApplyTo pins ValidAlgorithms to the algorithms of the keys actually loaded, so a token cannot pick its own (none, or HS256 presented against the public key).
  • Once an asymmetric key is configured, Jwt:Key is no longer accepted for validation, even if it is still set. Jwt:AcceptLegacySymmetric=true re-admits it for a migration window; turn it off when the tokens signed with the old key have expired.
  • Startup fails on: more than one of the three asymmetric settings, a Jwt:JwksUrl that is not an absolute https URL, a private key in Jwt:PublicKeyPem, a key that is not P-256, or the legacy window switched on with no Jwt:Key.
  • The DB-backed configuration source cannot supply Jwt:SigningKeyPem, Jwt:PublicKeyPem, Jwt:JwksUrl or Jwt:AcceptLegacySymmetric (they are protected keys, like Jwt:Key).

docs.title: Publishing and following keys (JWKS)
docs.text:
An issuer publishes the public half of its signing key as a JSON Web Key Set; ExportJwks() returns the document (never private or symmetric material — a host signing with Jwt:Key publishes an empty set):

var jwks = keys.ExportJwks();
app.MapGet("/.well-known/jwks.json", () => Results.Content(jwks, "application/json")).AllowAnonymous();

A validator sets Jwt:JwksUrl to that address instead of copying a PEM. What to expect:

Situation Behaviour Normal operation The key set is fetched on first use, cached, and re-fetched hourly. A token arrives with an unknown kid (the issuer rotated) That request gets 401 and triggers a re-fetch (at most one every 30 s); the next request is accepted. To rotate without that one 401, publish the new key before signing with it. The issuer has withdrawn a key It stops being accepted as soon as the set is re-fetched — there is no fallback to the previous set. The issuer cannot be reached, a key set was fetched earlier The current set keeps working. The issuer cannot be reached, nothing was fetched yet Every token is refused (401) until a fetch succeeds. The document contains other keys (symmetric, RSA, another curve, a private part, use ≠ sig) They are ignored; a document with no usable key counts as a failed fetch.

FromConfiguration(configuration, jwksClient) takes the HttpClient used for the fetch — pass one to set a timeout or, in development, to accept a local certificate.

  • Jwt:AdditionalPublicKeysPem (up to four PUBLIC KEY blocks, beside Jwt:SigningKeyPem or Jwt:PublicKeyPem) lists further accepted keys. An issuer also publishes them, which is how a signing key is rotated without a failed request: publish the next key first, switch, keep the previous one until its tokens have expired — see Secret rotation. It is refused beside Jwt:JwksUrl or a symmetric-only key, and a database config row cannot supply it.
  • Generate a pair with asdamir secrets new-signing-key. A PEM stored on one line with literal \n separators (an environment variable) is read as-is.

docs.title: An app's own service key
docs.text:
A Gateway also authenticates itself to the control plane — for the central log and the agent-audit ledger — with a short-lived service token (AppLogServiceToken, AgentAuditServiceToken). Signed with the shared Jwt:Key, such a token could be produced by any holder of that key for any app. With a service key, it can only speak for the app that owns the key:

  • The app generates its own EC P-256 pair (asdamir secrets new-signing-key). The private key goes to that app's Gateway as App:ServiceKeyPem (a secret; a database config row cannot supply it). The public key is registered with the control plane against the app — on the console's Apps screen, or with PUT /api/admin/apps/{appId}/service-key.
  • AppServiceKey.FromPem(pem).SigningCredentials signs ES256, and both Mint methods have an overload taking those credentials. The two sinks do this for you: set AppLogForwardOptions.ServiceKeyPem / AgentAuditOptions.ServiceKeyPem (AgentAudit:ServiceKeyPem) and they stop using the shared key.
  • The control plane verifies a service token against the key registered for the app_code the token names — another app's key does not verify it, and neither does the control plane's own key.
Situation Behaviour The app has no key registered Its service tokens under the shared key are accepted, as before. The app has a key registered Only tokens signed with that key are accepted. A token for this app under the shared key is refused. A token is signed with a key that is not registered for that app 401. Two keys are registered Both are accepted — register the new key beside the old one, switch the Gateway, then remove the old one (up to four keys). A key is removed, or the app is deactivated Its tokens are refused from the next request. App:ServiceKeyPem is set but unreadable The sink sends nothing and reports it; it does not fall back to the shared key.

A service key signs service tokens only: it cannot produce an end-user or an operator token.

docs.title: The orchestration token
docs.text:
When the control plane calls a managed app's gateway/admin/* endpoints it presents an orchestration token (OrchestrationToken, Core). It signs the token with its own key, so the Gateway verifies it against the same published keys as a user token — no secret is exchanged and the Gateway stores none.

Property Value Why Audience Jwt:OrchestrationAudience (default asdamir-app-orchestration) Not the user audience and not the console audience: no user endpoint and no control-plane endpoint accepts it. token_use orchestration Marks what it is. app_code the one app being called A Gateway that receives it cannot replay it against another app. client_id admin-console by default The Gateway's AppMgmtClient policy authorizes this value (AdminConsole:ClientId). Lifetime 5 minutes

The token carries no tenant (tid): the control plane belongs to none. Under strict tenancy an endpoint it calls must be marked [AllowWithoutTenant], or the tenant middleware answers 403 tenant.unresolved after authentication succeeds — see multi-tenancy.

A Gateway calls OrchestrationToken.IsFor(principal, appCode, audience) for any token carrying client_id and fails authentication when it returns false; a generated Gateway does this already.

docs.title: What a generated app is given
docs.text:
asdamir new app wires the above for you:

App Token validation Service key Commercial (default) No key of its own. With none of Jwt:JwksUrl / Jwt:PublicKeyPem / Jwt:Key set, the Gateway uses <AdminConsole:BaseUrl>/.well-known/jwks.json. Generated: the private key is in the Gateway's user-secrets (App:ServiceKeyPem), the public key in register_<app>.sql. Free (--mode free) Its own Jwt:Key — it issues and validates its own tokens, and shares the key with nothing. None: there is no control plane to authenticate to.

A commercial Gateway therefore holds nothing that can mint a user or operator token. It needs the control plane to sign with Jwt:SigningKeyPem; a control plane still signing with Jwt:Key publishes no key and the Gateway rejects every token.

docs.title: Refresh tokens
docs.text:
The management app demonstrates the recommended pattern (see Asdamir.AdminConsole.Api/Auth):

  • Refresh tokens are SHA-256 hashed before storage — the raw token never touches the database.
  • Rotation on use: every refresh issues a new token and invalidates the old one. The spend is atomic — when two requests present the same token at once, exactly one is rotated.
  • Reuse detection: presenting an already-rotated token revokes the user's entire token tree (theft response). The loser of a concurrent race is a second spend like any other and is handled the same way, so a client must serialize its own refreshes (one refresh in flight per session).
  • Context binding: a refresh token is redeemable only where it was issued — a console token at the console refresh endpoint, an app token at that app's app-refresh.
  • Expiry is checked against DateTime.UtcNow.

docs.title: Sign-out and forced session end
docs.text:
• POST api/admin/auth/logout takes an optional { "refreshToken": "…" } body. With it, only that session's refresh token is revoked (the user's other browsers/devices stay signed in); without a body, every refresh token of the user is revoked ("sign out everywhere").
  • An administrator resetting a user's password or deactivating a user revokes all of that user's refresh tokens and ends their live console sessions immediately — the account stops working at once rather than when its tokens expire. Re-activating a user grants nothing back; they sign in again.
  • A self-service password reset (reset-password) and a password change also revoke every refresh token of the user.

docs.title: Per-app login (mobile token flow)
docs.text:
Managed apps (web + mobile) don't own users — identity is central. Each app's Gateway proxies credentials to AppManagement, which validates them, checks the user's access to that app (dbo.UserAppRoles) and issues an app-scoped token (permissions are exactly the user's roles on that app, never the admin pool):

Gateway endpoint → AppManagement Purpose gateway/auth/login api/admin/auth/app-login email + password (+ App:Code) → token pair gateway/auth/twofactor/verify api/admin/auth/app-twofactor/verify complete 2FA → token pair gateway/auth/refresh api/admin/auth/app-refresh rotate the refresh token → fresh app-scoped token pair gateway/auth/forgot-password api/admin/auth/forgot-password request a reset link (always 200)

The Gateway injects the app's App:Code so the token is scoped to it.

Mobile token storage & auto-refresh. The MAUI app keeps the tokens in SecureStorage (ITokenStore), not a cookie. MobileApiClient stamps the bearer on every call; on a 401 it calls gateway/auth/refresh once, retries the request, and — if the refresh also fails — clears the tokens and routes to /login. See Mobile App.

docs.title: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
docs.text:
ITwoFactorService issues and verifies a short-lived challenge:

  • Challenge tokens use a 128-bit CSPRNG value (RandomNumberGenerator), Base64URL-encoded — not a GUID.
  • A successful password step returns Required = true + a challenge token; the client completes the second factor against the 2FA endpoint.
  • A challenge is bound to the sign-in surface that created it — console, or app:<code> for a managed app. It can only be redeemed at that surface's verify endpoint: a code issued for an app sign-in can never complete a console sign-in (or another app's), and is refused exactly like an unknown token.
  • The console verify step re-checks the operator gate and the lockout state itself — it is the endpoint that issues the token, so it does not rely on the password step having asked.
  • A wrong code counts toward account lockout exactly like a wrong password, and the failed-attempt counter is cleared only when authentication is complete (after the code step for a 2FA user).
  • Delivery: outside Development the code is sent by SMS through the transactional outbox; the message body is the TwoFactor:SmsTemplate setting ({0} = the code), with a built-in default. In Development the code is only logged, never sent.
  • A 2FA-enabled user without a phone number cannot sign in outside Development: a challenge nobody can answer is not issued, and the login is refused with the same opaque failure as a wrong password.
  • Code lifetime defaults to 180 seconds (Security.Otp.TtlMinutes, default 3, clamped to 30 s – 30 min) — the same value the login page counts down.

docs.title: Blazor: auth state & token propagation
docs.text:
In a Blazor app, Asdamir.Web provides the authentication-state provider and bearer-token propagation:

builder.Services.AddSecurityAuthenticationState();
builder.Services.AddSecurityHttpClient();   // attaches the bearer token to outbound API calls
builder.Services.AddSecurityAutoLogout();   // idle/auto-logout + session activity tracking

The AdminConsole stores the access token in an HttpOnly cookie and attaches it as a bearer on outbound API calls via a cookie→bearer handler.

The Blazor host holds no Jwt:Key (secrets live on the API tier), so it never trusts a claim it reads out of a token it was handed. Before it creates the cookie session it presents the token to the API (GET api/admin/auth/me) and builds the cookie principal from the API's answer; a rejected token — or an API that cannot be reached — means no session (fail closed). Each cookie session is identified by a random, server-minted session id (the sid claim), not by the user id, so two browsers of the same user are independent sessions: each keeps its own rotating refresh token, and signing out of one leaves the other alone. The server-side session map is in-memory and single-node; after a restart it is rebuilt from the cookies.

docs.title: Login failure hygiene
docs.text:
All login failures (unknown email, locked account, wrong password) return the same opaque response to avoid username-enumeration. Lockout state is enforced server-side but never disclosed in the response body.

The anonymous auth endpoints are rate limited per client IP, each in its own bucket, overridable through RateLimiting:<Bucket>:PermitLimit / RateLimiting:<Bucket>:WindowSeconds:

Bucket Endpoints Default Login login, app-login 5 per 60 s TwoFactorSend twofactor/verify, app-twofactor/verify 3 per 60 s Refresh refresh, app-refresh 10 per 60 s ForgotPassword forgot-password 5 per 60 s ResetPassword reset-password 5 per 60 s

docs.title: Upgrade notes
docs.text:
• Operators sign in once more after upgrading the AdminConsole. A console cookie issued before sessions carried a sid claim is rejected; the next request lands on the login page.
  • Apply the database migrations before deploying the new API build. Atomic refresh rotation and context-bound 2FA challenges rely on schema objects the new build calls; a 2FA challenge started by the previous build is not redeemable by the new one (it expires within minutes — the user simply signs in again).
  • A 2FA-enabled account needs a phone number outside Development, or it can no longer sign in.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: Packages: Asdamir.Core (permission/policy constants), Asdamir.Web (route authorization, audit)

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Authorization in Asdamir is permission-based: roles are granted permissions, policies map to those permissions, and endpoints/pages require a policy. The framework adds route-level authorization, an authorization cache and an authorization audit trail on top of ASP.NET Core's primitives.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddBasicAuthorization();        // policy + permission plumbing
// or, with the enterprise add-ons (cache, audit, rate-limited checks):
builder.Services.AddEnterpriseAuthorization();

docs.title: Permissions & policies
docs.text:
Permission and policy names are centralized as constants in Asdamir.Core.Authorization:

using Asdamir.Core.Authorization;

[Authorize(Policy = PolicyNames.ProductsRead)]
public IActionResult List() => ...;

Define permissions once and reference them everywhere — this keeps endpoint guards, role definitions and the admin UI in sync.

docs.title: Route authorization (Blazor / middleware)
docs.text: Asdamir.Web.Security provides route-level authorization so unauthenticated/unauthorized navigation is blocked before a page renders, plus components such as AuthorizeView, AuthenticationGuard and AccessDenied. Authorization decisions are cached (route-normalized — the query string is stripped so high-cardinality URLs don't explode the cache) and can be audited.

docs.title: Two-tier RBAC (AdminConsole)
docs.text:
The management application layers two independent RBAC scopes:

  1. Admin-pool RBAC — gates which managed apps an operator may administer. SuperAdmins reach every app; everyone else reaches only the apps assigned to them. Being assigned to an app grants read access; changing its configuration, localization, roles, role assignments, outbox messages or jobs additionally requires the matching write permission.
  2. Managed-app RBAC — each managed app defines its own roles, permissions and role assignments for its end users.

See Architecture → Security & multi-tenancy.

docs.title: Authorization audit
docs.text: Authorization decisions (grants and denials) can be written to the audit trail for security review — see Audit Logging.

docs.text: • Authentication · Web Security · Audit Logging

docs.title: Background Jobs
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Data · Namespace: Asdamir.Data.HangfireJobs

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Asdamir runs background and scheduled work on Hangfire, with a thin framework layer that gives jobs a uniform contract, a DI-resolvable executor and a dashboard.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddCoreHangfireJobs(builder.Configuration);
...
app.UseCoreHangfireApi();        // JSON monitoring endpoints
app.UseCoreHangfireDashboard();  // Hangfire dashboard (guard it behind auth!)

docs.title: Writing a job
docs.text:
Implement IJob and return a JobResult — return failure, don't swallow it:

public sealed class NightlyReconcileJob : IJob
{
    public string Name => nameof(NightlyReconcileJob);

    public async Task<JobResult> ExecuteAsync(IJobContext ctx, CancellationToken ct = default)
    {
        try
        {
            await ReconcileAsync(ct);
            return JobResult.Success(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2));
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            return JobResult.Failure(ex.Message);   // re-thrown so Hangfire retry fires
        }
    }
}

A failing JobResult is re-thrown by the executor so Hangfire marks the job failed and applies AutomaticRetry — a job that "logs and returns success" hides outages.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Use the scheduler abstraction to enqueue or schedule recurring jobs by type:

public sealed class Bootstrap(IJobScheduler jobs)
{
    public Task ConfigureAsync() => jobs.RecurringAsync<NightlyReconcileJob>("0 2 * * *"); // 02:00 daily
}

IJobScheduler (Asdamir.Data.HangfireJobs) schedules by job type — RecurringAsync<T>, ScheduleAsync, RemoveRecurringAsync. The lower-level IHangfireJobService (Asdamir.Core.Contracts) takes a method-call expression instead: Enqueue<T>(x => x.Run()), Schedule<T>(…, delay), Recurring<T>(jobId, x => x.Run(), cron).

docs.title: Per-app isolation (multi-company)
docs.text:
When several apps share one company's Hangfire schema, configure HangfireJobsOptions so each app stays isolated (per the AppManagement multi-company design):

  • AppQueue (e.g. the app's Code) — enqueued, delayed (scheduled) and recurring jobs all route to this queue and the app's worker listens only on it, so one app's job surge can't starve another and another app's worker never picks up this app's delayed job.
  • RecurringJobIdPrefix — recurring ids become {prefix}:{jobId}, so two apps can both define e.g. daily-cleanup without colliding. RemoveRecurringAsync applies the same prefix: pass either the id you gave RecurringAsync or the effective (already prefixed) id it returned — the prefix is never applied twice.

Both default to empty → Hangfire's default queue (unchanged single-app behaviour). Each generated app runs its own Hangfire server; cross-company isolation is automatic (separate company DB = separate schema).

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: The AdminConsole surfaces job state (enqueued/processing/succeeded/failed) and lets operators requeue or delete jobs — it observes only and hosts no workers itself.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • Transactional Outbox — for reliable message delivery, prefer the outbox over ad-hoc jobs

docs.title: Background Runs
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core (abstraction) · Asdamir.Data (implementation) · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.BackgroundRuns / Asdamir.Data.BackgroundRuns

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Some operations are too heavy to run inside an HTTP request — a 100k×100k reconciliation, a bulk import, a large export. The background-run primitive gives the API/Gateway tier a reusable facility to trigger → run in the background → query status/progress: a controller enqueues a run and returns its id immediately; callers poll for lifecycle and progress.

The framework manages the run lifecycle and persistence; the job's content is app-defined. This means an existing engine — e.g. an IReconciliationEngine.RunAsync(...) — is wrapped without any signature change; writing the wrapping handler is the application's job.

This is distinct from Background Jobs (Hangfire — recurring/scheduled fire-and-forget work) and the Transactional Outbox (reliable mail/SMS). Reach for a background run when a caller needs to trigger a one-off long operation and watch its progress.

docs.title: Why not Hangfire?
docs.text: A generated Gateway registers no Hangfire server (Hangfire lives in AppManagement's job tier). Hangfire also has no first-class per-run progress query against the app's own schema. So the primitive ships its own runner — a BackgroundService + an in-process channel (no external broker) — plus DB-persisted run state you can query. It mirrors the choice AppManagement.Api already makes (a BackgroundService, not a Hangfire server).

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
One line in the Gateway Program.cs, then one handler per job type:

builder.Services.AddDataAccess(connString);   // IDbConnectionFactory
builder.Services.AddMultiTenancy();           // ITenantContext (runs are tenant-scoped)

builder.Services.AddBackgroundRuns(builder.Configuration);   // service + runner + restart-recovery + store
builder.Services.AddBackgroundJob<ReconciliationJobHandler>(); // one per JobType

AddBackgroundRuns picks the Dapper store or the InMemory store from Persistence:UseInMemory, registers the hosted runner and the startup restart-recovery service, and binds BackgroundRunOptions from the BackgroundRuns configuration section (DB-backed AppConfigurations, never hardcoded).

docs.title: The API surface
docs.text:
public interface IBackgroundRunService
{
    Task<Guid> EnqueueAsync(BackgroundRunRequest req, CancellationToken ct = default);
    Task<BackgroundRunStatus?> GetStatusAsync(Guid runId, CancellationToken ct = default);
}

public sealed record BackgroundRunRequest(
    string JobType, string? Payload = null, string? DedupKey = null, bool AllowConcurrent = false);

public sealed record BackgroundRunStatus(
    Guid RunId, string JobType, BackgroundRunState State,
    int? ProgressCompleted, int? ProgressTotal, string? ResultRef, string? ErrorSummary,
    DateTime CreatedAtUtc, DateTime? StartedAtUtc, DateTime? CompletedAtUtc);

public enum BackgroundRunState { Pending, Running, Completed, Failed, Interrupted }

public interface IBackgroundJobHandler   // the app-supplied job BODY
{
    string JobType { get; }
    Task<string?> ExecuteAsync(BackgroundRunContext context);   // one context, not loose params
}

public sealed record BackgroundRunContext(   // everything the runner knows about the run
    Guid RunId, string TenantId, string? Payload,
    IProgressReporter Progress, CancellationToken CancellationToken);

docs.title: Run context
docs.text:
The handler receives ONE BackgroundRunContext rather than loose parameters, so future fields extend the context without another signature break:

Field Meaning RunId The store record's run id — identical to the value EnqueueAsync returned and GetStatusAsync(runId).RunId reports. TenantId The run's tenant; the runner has already re-established ambient tenant scope from it. Payload The opaque input from BackgroundRunRequest.Payload (typically JSON), or null. Progress The cheap, throttled progress sink (call Report(done, total) per unit of work). CancellationToken Cooperative cancellation for shutdown / abort — honour it.

RunId is the two-way back-link. Because context.RunId is the same id the caller holds, the handler can persist it on its own business record (e.g. a domain "run" row) so traceability goes both ways — the framework's BackgroundRuns row points at nothing app-specific, but the app row points back at the run, closing the audit / maker-checker loop. A forward-reference-only design (before the context) could not do this: the handler never saw its own RunId.

A controller triggers and polls:

[HttpPost("reconciliations")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Start([FromBody] StartDto dto, CancellationToken ct)
{
    var runId = await _runs.EnqueueAsync(
        new BackgroundRunRequest("reconciliation", Payload: JsonSerializer.Serialize(dto), DedupKey: dto.Period), ct);
    return Accepted(new { runId });
}

[HttpGet("reconciliations/{runId:guid}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Status(Guid runId, CancellationToken ct)
    => await _runs.GetStatusAsync(runId, ct) is { } s ? Ok(s) : NotFound();

docs.title: Lifecycle & state machine
docs.text:
Pending ──▶ Running ──▶ Completed
                  └────▶ Failed
(Pending|Running) ──▶ Interrupted   (restart-recovery only)

Transitions are guarded and WHERE-scoped (mirroring the AppManagement proc convention: SET NOCOUNT ON + SELECT @@ROWCOUNT) — an illegal transition affects 0 rows and returns false. The app handler never sets state directly: it returns (optionally a ResultRef) on success, or throws on failure — a thrown exception is what moves the run to Failed with the error recorded. Honour the supplied CancellationToken.

docs.title: Progress (throttled / batched)
docs.text:
The handler reports via a cheap IProgressReporter.Report(completed, total) that it can call per row. The reporter coalesces in memory and flushes to the store at most:

  • once per ProgressFlushIntervalMs (default 750 ms), or
  • once per ProgressFlushPercentStep advance of the total (default 5%, so short jobs still move).

So 100k Report calls become a handful of DB writes, not 100k. Progress writes are advisory (fire-and-forget; a flush failure never fails the run), and the final value is force-flushed just before a terminal transition so no progress is lost.

docs.title: Concurrency policy
docs.text: With the default (AllowConcurrent = false), enqueuing a run whose (JobType + DedupKey) already has a Pending/Running run for the tenant does not start a duplicate — it returns the existing RunId. Set AllowConcurrent = true to always start a fresh run. The runner also bounds parallelism with BackgroundRunOptions.MaxConcurrency (default 2).

docs.title: Persistence, tenancy & restart-recovery
docs.text:
Runs are persisted — in-memory-only is forbidden in production. The dbo.BackgroundRuns table lives in the app's OWN business database (this is app-operational state, not central management data, per the CENTRAL rule — it is not in AsdamirVault). Every read/write is tenant-scoped: tenant A's runs are invisible to tenant B.

On startup, a restart-recovery IHostedService flips every run left Pending/Running by a prior process that died to Interrupted — so no ghost "Running" survives a restart. (Verified by an integration test: seed a Running row, run recovery, assert it becomes Interrupted.)

docs.title: HA — known limitation
docs.text: The primitive assumes a single node. Multi-node leader election / distributed run ownership is not solved here: startup recovery would wrongly mark a peer's live runs Interrupted, and the in-process queue is per-process. A scale-out deployment needs a shared/distributed run owner — the same caveat as the in-memory session store. (OwnerToken is recorded on a Running row so this can be built on later.)

docs.title: Wrapping an existing engine (the hook)
docs.text:
A handler wraps an existing RunAsync-style engine without changing its signature — the framework owns the lifecycle, the engine owns the work:

public sealed class ReconciliationJobHandler(IReconciliationEngine engine) : IBackgroundJobHandler
{
    public string JobType => "reconciliation";

    public async Task<string?> ExecuteAsync(BackgroundRunContext context)
    {
        var req = JsonSerializer.Deserialize<ReconRequest>(context.Payload!)!;     // decode app input
        req.BackgroundRunId = context.RunId;                                       // back-link: my record -> the run row
        var result = await engine.RunAsync(req, onProgress: (done, total) =>       // engine signature UNCHANGED
            context.Progress.Report(done, total), context.CancellationToken);      // just forward progress
        return result.ReportId.ToString();                                         // stored as ResultRef
    }
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Key Default Purpose BackgroundRuns:MaxConcurrency 2 Max runs executed at once by the runner BackgroundRuns:ProgressFlushIntervalMs 750 Min gap between progress flushes BackgroundRuns:ProgressFlushPercentStep 5 Also flush every this-percent advance BackgroundRuns:NodeId {Machine}#{Pid} Owner token recorded on a Running row

Bind these from AppConfigurations (see Configuration); do not hardcode them.

docs.title: Billing
docs.text:
Billing is an opt-in feature family: a generated app can host an end-user payment page so its own users can subscribe and pay. It is off by default — without the flag, not a single billing file is emitted and a generated app is byte-identical to one scaffolded without it.

asdamir new app MyApp --billing            # commercial (Model A)
asdamir new app MyApp --mode free --billing  # free / self-contained (Model B)

Both add an end-user page at /billing — plans, the current subscription, and checkout.

docs.title: Two models
docs.text:
Billing follows the same commercial vs free split as the rest of the framework:

Model A — commercial (--billing) Model B — free (--mode free --billing) Where billing data lives Central AsdamirVault, scoped by the app's AppId The app's own database (single-tenant) Payment secret Held centrally by AppManagement (the app never sees it) The app owns its own Payment:Paddle:* config How the app serves it Gateway proxies gateway/billing/* → AppManagement Gateway serves billing locally via the Asdamir.Payments package (LocalDbBillingStore + a local webhook) Operator view Monitored from AppManagement's /billing console No control plane — the app owns it end to end

In both models the end-user page is identical; only the wiring behind it differs.

docs.title: Payment rails
docs.text:
Billing is provider-agnostic behind IPaymentProvider. Two rails ship in Asdamir.Payments:

  • Paddle — Merchant of Record (default). Card / Apple Pay / Google Pay via Paddle's hosted checkout. Paddle is the Merchant of Record, so tax/VAT and invoicing are handled by Paddle (pass-through — the framework is not in the money path). Each tenant connects its own Paddle account; checkout redirects to that tenant's Paddle hosted page. Webhooks are signature-verified before any subscription state changes.
  • Crypto — default-off. A crypto rail exists behind the same IPaymentProvider contract but ships disabled (Payment:Crypto:Enabled=false) and is not Merchant-of-Record. Keep it off unless your finance/legal setup explicitly allows it.

docs.title: Subscription lifecycle
docs.text: Webhook events (checkout completed, renewed, cancelled, payment failed) are turned into subscription status transitions by the billing webhook processor. Recurring renewals and lifecycle transitions are driven by a background worker on the API tier, so a subscription's state stays current without a user action.

docs.title: Operator console (/billing) — commercial
docs.text: In commercial mode, operators monitor billing from AppManagement's /billing page: per-app subscriptions and their status, and each app's Paddle configuration (keys are seeded empty + encrypted by seed_billing.sql, then set from AppManagement — checkout goes live once they're set). Because the app proxies to AppManagement, the generated app never holds the payment secret.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: The Payment:Paddle:* (and Payment:Crypto:*) keys are seeded into AppConfigurations — empty and encrypted — by the billing seed (seed_billing.sql for Model A, a V*__freemode_billing_* migration for Model B). Set the real keys via AppManagement (Model A) or the app's own user-secrets / env (Model B). Never put a payment secret in appsettings.json.

docs.title: Localization
docs.text: The billing page's strings (Menu.Billing, Billing.Page.*) are seeded in all three cultures (tr-TR / en-US / ru-RU) by the billing seed, like any other generated feature.

docs.title: Configuration & Feature Flags
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Data · Namespace: Asdamir.Data.Configuration

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Beyond appsettings.json, Asdamir supports database-backed dynamic configuration: settings and feature flags that operators change at runtime — per tenant — without a redeploy. Values are layered on top of the standard .NET configuration system and cached for performance.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddFeatureManager(builder.Configuration);

This wires the IFeatureManager, the dynamic configuration source and its caching.

docs.title: Feature flags & typed configuration
docs.text:
public sealed class CheckoutService(IFeatureManager features)
{
    public async Task CheckoutAsync(string? tenantId)
    {
        if (await features.IsEnabledAsync("BulkOrdering", tenantId))
        {
            var cfg = await features.GetConfigurationAsync<DiscountConfig>("OrderDiscounts", tenantId);
            // apply tenant-specific configuration …
        }
    }
}
  • IsEnabledAsync(name, tenantId?) — check a flag globally or for a specific tenant.
  • GetConfigurationAsync<T>(key, tenantId?) — fetch and deserialize typed configuration.

A null tenantId reads the global value; a tenant value overrides the global one (see Multi-Tenancy).

docs.title: Dynamic configuration provider
docs.text: AddFeatureManager also contributes an IConfigurationProvider that surfaces database values through IConfiguration, so existing IOptions<T> bindings can read DB-managed settings. Refreshes are cached to keep the hot path cheap.

docs.title: Per-app DB configuration (AppConfigurations)
docs.text:
Each app keeps its runtime settings per application in dbo.AppConfigurations ([Key]/[Value]/[Category], AppId-scoped). The API tier registers that table into IConfiguration at startup with builder.Configuration.AddDatabaseConfiguration(...) (loads the active rows of the configured scope, refreshes on an interval — see below), so the values are reachable like any other config (Configuration["Key"], Configure<TOptions>(GetSection(...))). The UI/client tier never touches the DB — a small endpoint serves the client-facing subset over HTTP (/gateway/client-settings).

Seeded keys include Session:IdleSeconds/Session:CountdownSeconds and the token lifetimes Jwt:AccessTokenLifetimeMinutes / Jwt:RefreshTokenLifetimeDays. AppManagement reads the latter from the issuing app's AppConfigurations when minting that app's JWTs (re-read per login/refresh, so a change applies without redeploy) — see Authentication.

docs.title: AddDatabaseConfiguration — scope, protected keys, failure behaviour
docs.text:
builder.Configuration.AddDatabaseConfiguration(connectionFactory, o =>
{
    o.AppId = myAppId;                              // load only this application's rows (+ global rows)
    o.RefreshInterval = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5);    // default
    // o.IncludeGlobal = true;                      // default — also load AppId IS NULL rows
    // o.ProtectedKeys.Add("MyHost:Secret");        // keys a database row may never supply
});

var app = builder.Build();
app.Configuration.AttachDatabaseConfigurationLogging(app.Services.GetRequiredService<ILoggerFactory>());
DatabaseConfigurationOptions Default Effect AppId null Set it whenever the table is shared between applications. Only rows with this AppId are loaded, plus the global (AppId IS NULL) rows; when both define a key, the application's own row wins. Another application's rows are never read. null reads the table unscoped (every active row, ordered by key) and does not reference the AppId column at all — for a table that belongs to one host alone. IncludeGlobal true With AppId set, also load the global rows. ProtectedKeys Jwt:Key, Security:EncryptionKey, ConnectionStrings:*, Persistence:UseInMemory Keys a database row can never supply — matching rows are dropped and reported through the logger. The DB source outranks appsettings / user-secrets / environment variables, so without this anyone able to write a config row could replace the signing key or a connection string. Matching is case-insensitive; an entry ending in :* protects the whole section. Add host-specific keys, or Clear() the set to opt out. Encryption null An IEncryptionService. When set, rows flagged IsEncrypted = 1 are decrypted before they reach IConfiguration (see below). When null, the IsEncrypted column is not read and values load exactly as stored. RefreshInterval 5 minutes How often the table is re-read.

The AddDatabaseConfiguration(connectionFactory, refreshInterval) overload is the unscoped form with the same default protected keys.

  • Only IsActive = 1 rows are loaded, and keys are case-insensitive (as IConfiguration keys are).
  • The first load is synchronous (one attempt, made when the configuration is built), so startup code that reads a DB-backed key sees it. If that first attempt fails the host still starts — without DB-backed values — and the refresh loop retries.
  • A failed reload keeps the last-known-good values. A transient database error never replaces good configuration with an empty set; the provider keeps serving what it has, retries on the next interval and logs the failure.
  • Logging is attached after Build(). Configuration is built before the host's logging exists, so call AttachDatabaseConfigurationLogging(...) once the host is built; it reports a load failure that happened in the meantime and any protected keys that were dropped. It is a no-op when no DB-backed provider is registered.

docs.title: Encrypted values (IsEncrypted)
docs.text:
builder.Configuration.AddDatabaseConfiguration(connectionFactory, o =>
{
    o.AppId = myAppId;
    // Built from the configuration available so far (environment / user-secrets):
    o.Encryption = new EncryptionService(builder.Configuration);
});

With Encryption set, each row flagged IsEncrypted = 1 is resolved on load, so every consumer — options binding included — receives the secret itself:

The row holds Result ciphertext (v2: prefix) that decrypts the plaintext is applied ciphertext that does not decrypt (wrong key, damaged value) the key is dropped and logged as an error (CONFIG_SECRET_UNDECRYPTABLE). Ciphertext is never passed on as if it were the secret, and a global row of the same key does not take its place a value that is not ciphertext applied as stored and logged as a warning — a secret sitting in plaintext an empty value stays empty (an unconfigured secret); nothing is logged

A row that is not flagged is never decrypted, whatever its value looks like. Security:EncryptionKey itself is a protected key: it must come from the environment or user-secrets, never from the table being read. Produce ciphertext with asdamir secrets encrypt, or let a writer that encrypts do it (the AppManagement console encrypts every value saved as secret). Without Encryption the provider behaves as it always did: no decrypt-on-load.

docs.title: Layering precedence
docs.text: Standard .NET precedence applies — later sources win. The database provider sits above static JSON so an operator override takes effect without touching files.

docs.title: Data Access
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Data · Namespace: Asdamir.Data, Asdamir.Core.Contracts

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Asdamir uses Dapper for data access — fast, explicit SQL with no change-tracking surprises — over a provider-agnostic connection abstraction so the same repository code runs against SQL Server, Oracle or PostgreSQL.

docs.title: Connection abstraction
docs.text:
IDbConnectionFactory (Asdamir.Core.Contracts) hands out open IDbConnections; IDbProvider describes the active database engine (DbProviderType). Repositories depend on the factory, not on a concrete provider:

public sealed class OrderRepository(IDbConnectionFactory factory)
{
    public async Task<Order?> GetAsync(Guid id)
    {
        using var conn = factory.Create();
        return await conn.QuerySingleOrDefaultAsync<Order>(
            "dbo.Order_Get", new { id }, commandType: CommandType.StoredProcedure);
    }
}

The management app uses an async factory variant (CreateAsync(ct)) for its stores; pick the shape that matches your hosting.

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Stored procedures over inline SQL where practical — the management app routes every operation through canonical dbo.* procs.
  • Wrap connections (and Dapper using var readers) in using so they're disposed deterministically.
  • Pass CancellationToken through CommandDefinition.

docs.title: Custom type handlers
docs.text: Register Dapper type handlers (e.g. JSON columns ⇄ string[]) once at startup. The management app ships a JsonStringArrayHandler as a reference.

docs.title: Migrations
docs.text:
Schema is managed with ordered SQL migration scripts. The CLI can scaffold a new migration:

dotnet run --project src/Asdamir.Tools -- entity new Order   # generates entity + repository + migration

docs.title: Encryption
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.Services, Asdamir.Core.Contracts

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Asdamir provides authenticated symmetric encryption for protecting sensitive values at rest (configuration secrets, stored tokens, PII columns). It uses modern AES-GCM with a key derived from your master key via PBKDF2, and keeps a read-only legacy path so existing data can be migrated transparently.

docs.title: IEncryptionService
docs.text:
public interface IEncryptionService
{
    string Encrypt(string plainText);
    string Decrypt(string cipherText);
    bool   IsEncrypted(string text);
}

public sealed class SecretStore(IEncryptionService crypto)
{
    public string Protect(string value)   => crypto.Encrypt(value);
    public string Reveal(string protec)    => crypto.Decrypt(protec);
    public bool   AlreadyProtected(string v) => crypto.IsEncrypted(v);
}

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• v2 (default): AES-GCM — authenticated encryption with a random per-message nonce and an auth tag, so tampering is detected on decrypt.
  • Legacy (read path): AES-CBC values written by older versions still decrypt, so you can re-encrypt on next write during a migration.
  • Key derivation: the symmetric key is derived from Security:EncryptionKey with PBKDF2 (Rfc2898DeriveBytes.Pbkdf2) — the configured key is a passphrase, not the raw AES key.

IsEncrypted lets call sites detect already-protected values (idempotent encrypt-on-save).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
// appsettings.json holds NO secret. Supply the key out-of-band:
//   dev : dotnet user-secrets set "Security:EncryptionKey" "<32+ char>"
//   prod: environment variable  Security__EncryptionKey

The key must be ≥ 32 characters. Rotating it is a data-migration event: values encrypted under the old key cannot be read under a new one, so decrypt-then-re-encrypt during rotation — use asdamir secrets rotate-key. See the Secret Management & Key Rotation runbook.

docs.title: Hashing
docs.text: CryptographyService provides hashing helpers used for non-reversible needs (e.g. the management app hashes refresh tokens with SHA-256 before storage — the raw token is never persisted). Use encryption for values you must read back, hashing for values you only need to compare.

docs.title: Related: Data Protection (web)
docs.text: For browser-facing token protection (email/refresh tokens in cookies), Asdamir.Web exposes ASP.NET Core Data Protection via DataProtectionService with keyed purposes — see Web Security.

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.ErrorHandling

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Asdamir favours explicit, structured errors over unhandled exceptions:

  • A functional Result type for expected failures.
  • A global exception middleware that converts anything uncaught into an RFC-7807 ProblemDetails response.
  • Multi-language error translation so clients receive a localized, safe message.
  • A dead-letter queue (DLQ) for failures that must not be lost.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddGlobalExceptionHandling();
...
app.UseGlobalExceptionHandling();   // place early so it wraps the whole pipeline

This is also included in the AddFramework() / UseFramework() umbrella.

docs.title: ProblemDetails mapping
docs.text:
Uncaught exceptions are mapped to a ProblemDetails body by IProblemDetailsMapper. The default mapper:

  • maps DomainException (and known infrastructure exceptions) to the right status code,
  • sets a stable type URN and an Extensions["code"] error code,
  • localizes the Title via the error-translation service,
  • never leaks raw exception messages, stack traces or backend/library versions.

If the response has already started when the exception surfaces (a streamed body, flushed headers), no error document can be written any more: the middleware still logs the exception in full and then rethrows, so the server aborts the connection rather than appending JSON to a half-sent body.

throw new DomainException("orders.not_found", "Order was not found.");
// → 404 ProblemDetails { type, title (localized), extensions.code = "orders.not_found" }

docs.title: The Result type
docs.text:
Use Result / Result<T> for expected, non-exceptional failures:

public async Task<Result<Order>> GetAsync(Guid id)
{
    var order = await _repo.FindAsync(id);
    return order is null
        ? Result<Order>.Fail("orders.not_found")
        : Result<Order>.Ok(order);
}

docs.title: Error translation
docs.text: IErrorTranslationService resolves an error key + language to a localized message, with fallbacks (requested culture → English → generic). Translations are sourced from the database, so operations can edit them without a redeploy.

docs.title: Dead-letter queue
docs.text: Failures that cannot be retried inline are written through IDlqWriter (a file-backed writer ships by default) so they can be inspected and replayed rather than silently dropped.

docs.title: Correlation
docs.text:
Every request carries a correlation ID (see Observability); it flows into logs, ProblemDetails and outbound HTTP calls so a single failure can be traced end-to-end.

An inbound X-Correlation-Id header is reused only when it looks like an id: at most 64 characters of ASCII letters, digits, ., _ or -. Anything else — an oversized value, control characters, a comma-joined multi-value header — is discarded and a new id is generated, because the value is echoed into the response header and every log line. A rejected value is replaced, not sanitised: a "cleaned" id would correlate with nothing upstream.

docs.title: Localization
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Web · Namespace: Asdamir.Web.Localization

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Asdamir localizes UI strings through an API-backed store rather than static .resx files, so translations are edited centrally (by operators, in the AdminConsole) and refreshed at runtime. It ships multi-culture support out of the box (TR / EN / RU) and caches resolved strings for performance.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• An IStringLocalizer-compatible localizer (ApiStringLocalizer) resolves keys against a central localization API.
  • Results are cached (LocalizationCacheRefresher) and refreshed when the source version changes.
  • Authority lives in the AdminConsole's database; managed apps read from it and cache locally.
  • The localization API client validates the server's TLS certificate. Validation is skipped only in Development — when ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT is exactly Development and the host's IHostEnvironment (when one is registered) also reports Development — so a developer's self-signed certificate works, and a warning is logged whenever it is skipped. That warning must never appear outside a developer machine.

docs.title: Usage in components
docs.text:
@inject IStringLocalizer<MyComponent> L

<FluentLabel>@L["Users.Title"]</FluentLabel>

Missing keys fall back gracefully (requested culture → default culture → the key itself) so the UI never shows blanks.

docs.title: Editing translations
docs.text: Operators manage keys and per-culture values in the AdminConsole Localization editor; changes propagate to managed apps via the orchestration sync push. There is no inline upsert/delete from consumer code — the central store is the single source of truth.

docs.title: Menu labels
docs.text: Nav menu items are composed centrally (dbo.Menus, per app/AppId) and localized, not rendered from the raw stored Name. The generated NavMenu derives a stable key from each item's Url — /order-items → Menu.OrderItems — and resolves L["Menu.<Slug>"], falling back to the raw Name only when no key is seeded. asdamir new page seeds the matching Menu.<Slug> key (all cultures) in its localize_<entity>.sql, so the menu label, page title and field labels all translate together when the culture changes.

docs.title: Scope: which application a string belongs to
docs.text:
Every row in LocalizationResource carries an AppId, and it decides who can read the string.

AppId Meaning Who reads it a managed app's id that application's own strings that app, through its Gateway the self-app id the AdminConsole's own strings the console only NULL global — inherited by every managed app every managed app; not the console

The console reads with AppId = SelfApp and therefore does not inherit global rows: its own strings are always stored against the self-app explicitly. That asymmetry is deliberate — it is what stops a row left global by one application from silently becoming part of the operator console's vocabulary.

NULL is empty by design, and nothing seeds it. AsdamirVault_137 moved every stranded row onto the self-app, and no migration writes a global row on purpose. The slot stays open because Localization_GetMapForApp genuinely implements inheritance and that mechanism is worth keeping for framework-wide strings — but a key that lands there by accident is invisible to the console and visible to every app at once, which is exactly the defect 137 repaired. If you seed a global row, mean it.

(AppId, Key, Culture) is unique. That mirrors the canonical writer's own MERGE key, so the same key can never exist twice for one scope — the state in which an edit updates one copy while a reader serves another, and a stale translation reads as a correct one.

docs.title: History, because the shape repeats
docs.text: AsdamirVault_033 mapped the self-app id to NULL on write, when NULL was the console's scope. AsdamirVault_080 moved the console's rows onto the self-app id and _082 taught the readers to filter on it — but the writer was never updated, so for 362 keys across eleven feature areas the console wrote to one place and read from another. Its screens rendered raw keys on every fresh install while every managed app inherited those same strings. AsdamirVault_137 completes 080; the scoping is covered by LocalizationScopeIntegrationTests and by an E2E guard that fails any page showing a raw key.

docs.title: Cultures
docs.text: The framework's error-translation fallbacks cover tr, en and ru; add cultures by seeding their rows in the localization store.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.Contracts, Asdamir.Core.Modules

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A module packages a feature as a self-registering, dynamically discoverable unit with a managed lifecycle. Modules let you compose an application from independent capabilities without hand-wiring every service in Program.cs.

docs.title: The IModule contract
docs.text:
public interface IModule
{
    string Name { get; }
    string Version { get; }
    IEnumerable<string> Dependencies => Array.Empty<string>();

    void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config);
    void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IHostEnvironment env);
    Task InitializeAsync(IServiceProvider services, CancellationToken ct = default) => Task.CompletedTask;
}

Lifecycle, in order:

  1. ConfigureServices — register services with the DI container (called before the provider is built).
  2. Configure — add middleware / map endpoints (called after the provider is built).
  3. InitializeAsync — async startup work (migrations, cache warm-up, connectivity checks). The default is a no-op.

Dependencies declares other module names that must load first; the loader resolves the order and rejects cycles.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddModuleSystem();

AddModuleSystem registers the ModuleLoader, which discovers IModule implementations and runs their lifecycle. Implement a module like this:

public sealed class TelemetryModule : IModule
{
    public string Name => "Telemetry";
    public string Version => "1.0.0";

    public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services, IConfiguration config)
        => services.AddSingleton<IMetricsSink, SqlMetricsSink>();

    public void Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IHostEnvironment env) { }
}

docs.title: Scaffolding a module
docs.text:
The CLI generates a ready-to-fill module project (abstraction, options, service, DI extension, README):

dotnet run --project src/Asdamir.Tools -- module new Telemetry

See the CLI guide.

docs.title: Multi-Tenancy
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.MultiTenancy

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Multi-tenancy lets one deployment serve many tenants while keeping their data and configuration isolated. Asdamir resolves the current tenant per request and exposes it through an ambient ITenantContext that any service can inject.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddMultiTenancy();
...
app.UseMultiTenancy();   // resolves the tenant early in the pipeline

UseMultiTenancy runs the configured resolver and populates ITenantContext for the rest of the request.

Order matters, and AddMultiTenancy() alone does nothing. A resolver that reads the authenticated user (ClaimsTenantResolver) only sees a populated HttpContext.User after UseAuthentication(), so place UseMultiTenancy() after it:

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseMultiTenancy();
app.UseAuthorization();

If UseMultiTenancy() is missing, the first code that reads ITenantContext.TenantId during a request fails with TenancyNotConfiguredException (a 500 — it is a host wiring defect). It no longer runs every request as one tenant.

docs.title: Resolving the tenant
docs.text:
A resolver implements ITenantResolver. Two implementations ship out of the box:

Resolver Source ClaimsTenantResolver the signed tid claim on the authenticated principal (TenantIds.ClaimType) HeaderTenantResolver a request header (e.g. X-Tenant-Id) — any caller can set it; do not use it as a security boundary

Provide your own by registering a custom ITenantResolver before AddMultiTenancy() (it registers the header resolver with TryAdd). A resolver that cannot identify a tenant returns an unresolved new TenantContext() — it does not invent one.

docs.title: There is no default tenant
docs.text:
A missing tenant is an error, not a fallback. With the default TenancyOptions.MissingTenant = Reject:

Situation Result Authenticated request, token has no tid 403, error code tenant.unresolved (TenantNotResolvedException), refused by the middleware before any endpoint runs Anonymous request (health, login) continues; reading TenantId on that request throws the same 403 Authenticated request, no tid, endpoint marked [AllowWithoutTenant] continues with an unresolved tenant; reading TenantId behind it throws the same 403 AddMultiTenancy() without UseMultiTenancy() 500 TenancyNotConfiguredException on first tenant read Outside a request (background job) ITenantContext is an unresolved, settable TenantContext; the job sets its tenant, reading it first throws

Where the tenant is only advisory (a cache key, a log tag), check ITenantContext.IsResolved instead of reading TenantId.

The issuer states the tenant. IJwtService.IssueTokens(..., tenantId: …) writes the tid claim. A deliberately single-tenant application passes TenantIds.Single ("default"), so its tokens say so explicitly; asdamir new app emits exactly that, and the generated sample rows use the same value. To serve several tenants, pass each user's tenant — nothing downstream changes. Seed error.tenant.unresolved for the user-facing message (the scaffold does, in all three cultures).

An endpoint for a caller that belongs to no tenant. Some endpoints serve the application as a whole and are called by a principal no tenant owns — a control plane reading the app's audit trail, for example. Mark such an endpoint (controller or action) with [AllowWithoutTenant]:

[Authorize(Policy = "AppMgmtClient")]
[AllowWithoutTenant]
[Route("gateway/admin")]
public sealed class AuditTrailController : ControllerBase { … }

The attribute removes the up-front refusal for that endpoint only. It supplies no tenant (code behind it that reads TenantId still gets the 403) and it authorizes nothing, so pair it with a policy that names the tenant-less caller. The middleware reads it from the matched endpoint: routing must have run before UseMultiTenancy(), which is the case in a WebApplication that does not call UseRouting() itself. Where it has not, the attribute is not seen and the request is refused. The generated Gateway's gateway/admin/audittrail carries it.

Opting out. A host that is single-tenant by design and cannot change its issuer may restore the old behaviour explicitly:

builder.Services.AddMultiTenancy(o =>
{
    o.MissingTenant = MissingTenantBehavior.UseDefault;   // every scope without a tenant → DefaultTenantId
    o.DefaultTenantId = "default";
});

This removes the tenant boundary for any token that lacks the claim; do not use it in a multi-tenant host.

docs.title: Upgrading from 1.x
docs.text:
Before 2.0 a request without a tenant silently ran as "default". After upgrading:

  1. Upgrade the token issuer first so tokens carry tid (for a commercial app that is AppManagement; a free-mode app issues its own — regenerate or add the tenantId: argument in its AuthController).
  2. Then upgrade the API. Tokens issued before step 1 are refused until the session refreshes.
  3. Custom ITenantContext implementations keep compiling (IsResolved has a default implementation). Code that relied on TenantContext.TenantId returning "" now gets an exception — check IsResolved.

docs.title: Using the tenant context
docs.text:
public sealed class ReportService(ITenantContext tenant)
{
    public Task<Report> BuildAsync()
    {
        var tenantId = tenant.TenantId;   // ambient, per-request
        // scope queries / configuration to this tenant …
    }
}

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
"Tenancy": {
  "HeaderName": "X-Tenant-Id"
}

Bind options through AddMultiTenancy (it accepts an optional Action<TenancyOptions>).

docs.title: Tenant-aware features
docs.text: Other building blocks honour the resolved tenant — for example database-backed configuration / feature flags can return tenant-specific values via IFeatureManager.GetConfigurationAsync<T>(key, tenantId).

docs.title: AppManagement: the company (firma) model
docs.text:
The framework primitives above (ITenantResolver/ITenantContext) are the generic, request-scoped tenant abstraction. AppManagement builds a concrete multi-company control plane on top of them — one management database per company, every app's admin data sliced by AppId:

Company (firma)                         one management DB per company
  └── App            (Apps row)         CLI-registered; `asdamir app register`
        └── User                        company-unique identity
              └── Permissions           role + menu, scoped by AppId (Tier-2)

How a request resolves its slice:

Dimension Carried by Resolved into Picks Company JWT company claim (chosen pre-login) ICompanyContext which management database (company-aware IDbConnectionFactory) App X-App-Id request header (chosen post-login) IAppContext which AppId slice of Roles/Permissions/Menus/AppConfig/Localization
  • Catalog. Companies + their (encrypted) connection strings live in a bootstrap catalog outside any company DB — config-backed today (ICompanyCatalog), with a Companies table as the DB-backed alternative. A single-company deployment degenerates to the lone ConnectionStrings:AsdamirVault, so nothing changes for one company.
  • Admin authz. AppManagement admins are company-level full authority (Users.IsFullAuthority) — no per-admin role/permission machinery. The role/permission/menu tables are exclusively Tier-2 (the managed apps' end-user RBAC), keyed by AppId.
  • Selection flow. open → pick company → login → pick app → AppId-scoped reads. Both pickers auto-hide when there's only one choice.
  • Background jobs. Apps sharing a company's single Hangfire schema isolate via a per-app queue
  • {appCode}:{jobName} recurring-id prefix (see Background Jobs).

Full multi-company architecture is covered in the AppManagement documentation.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.ErrorHandling

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Asdamir ships structured logging and request correlation so a single user action can be traced across the UI, the API and downstream calls.

docs.title: Structured logging (Serilog)
docs.text:
Serilog is wired by the framework with console, file and SQL Server sinks plus enrichers (application name, correlation id). Bootstrap it early so even startup failures are captured:

// Serilog is configured by the framework's bootstrap; the application name
// comes from the LOG_APPLICATION environment variable (defaults to "Asdamir").
builder.Host.UseSerilog(...);   // see SerilogBootstrap

Log levels per namespace are controlled from configuration, e.g.:

"Serilog": { "MinimumLevel": { "Override": { "Asdamir.AdminConsole.Api.Outbox.Worker": "Debug" } } }

docs.title: Correlation IDs
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddCorrelationIdAccessor();

A correlation-ID middleware assigns/propagates an id per request and pushes it into the Serilog LogContext. CorrelationIdForwardingHandler attaches it to outbound HttpClient calls, and it appears in ProblemDetails responses — so one id ties the UI request, the API logs and the downstream call together.

public sealed class MyService(ICorrelationIdAccessor correlation)
{
    public void Work() => _logger.LogInformation("processing {CorrelationId}", correlation.CorrelationId);
}

docs.title: Database log sink & app log service
docs.text: IAppLogService writes application log entries to the database (with a Serilog fallback), powering the AdminConsole's log views without scraping files.

docs.title: Central error visibility for generated apps (the forward sink)
docs.text:
Every tier writes three Serilog sinks: Console + File + a central dbo.AppLog — but how the central sink is reached differs by tier, because a generated app must never write to the control-plane database directly (the layered / central-data rule):

  • The control plane (AppManagement's API) owns the log database, so its third sink writes directly to dbo.AppLog.
  • A generated app's Gateway cannot touch that database. Its third sink is AppLogForwardSink (in Asdamir.Data.Logging): it forwards Warning and above to the control plane's authenticated ingest endpoint (POST api/admin/applogs/ingest) over HTTP. The endpoint resolves which app the row belongs to from the Gateway's app-log service token — never from the request body — so one app can only write into its own log slice, and a forged app id is impossible.

The forward sink is built to never get in the app's way:

  • Fail-safe, not fail-open. If the control plane is down or slow, the sink swallows the error and keeps writing Console + File. A dropped log line is acceptable; a blocked or crashed app is not.
  • No feedback loop. It never forwards its own HTTP-transport log events, so a failing forward can't create a log storm.
  • Batched and bounded. Events go through an in-memory queue (async System.Threading.Channels) and are posted in batches; when the queue is full the oldest entry is dropped (with a one-time warning) rather than blocking the caller.

Configuration. The forward is on by default and opt-out per app:

// appsettings.json — generated Gateway
"AppLog": { "ForwardToCentral": true }   // set false to keep logs local only

Free mode (self-contained apps) has no control plane to forward to, so only Console + File are wired — there is no forward sink.

docs.title: Distributed tracing & metrics (OpenTelemetry)
docs.text:
Serilog owns logs; OpenTelemetry adds traces and metrics. The API tiers — AppManagement's API and every generated app's Gateway — emit:

  • Traces: incoming ASP.NET Core requests + outbound HttpClient calls (AppManagement → managed-app Gateways, Gateway → AppManagement), so one trace id follows a request across tiers.
  • Metrics: ASP.NET Core + HttpClient + .NET runtime (GC, thread pool, exceptions).

Everything is exported over OTLP to any collector (OpenTelemetry Collector, Jaeger, Tempo, Prometheus via the collector, Grafana, Azure Monitor, …).

docs.title: Enabling it (opt-in)
docs.text:
Tracing/metrics turn on only when an OTLP endpoint is configured, so local/dev/test runs without a collector stay quiet:

// appsettings.json (or env)
"OpenTelemetry": {
  "ServiceName": "my-app-gateway",        // optional; defaults to the assembly/project name
  "Otlp": { "Endpoint": "http://otel-collector:4317" }
}

The standard OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT environment variable is honoured too (handy for k8s sidecar/collector injection) — set either one. Empty/unset = OpenTelemetry is not registered (Serilog logging is unaffected).

docs.title: What's wired
docs.text:
AddOpenTelemetry().WithTracing(…).WithMetrics(…) with AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation(), AddHttpClientInstrumentation(), AddSqlClientInstrumentation() (traces), AddRuntimeInstrumentation() (metrics) and AddOtlpExporter(). The resource carries the service name + assembly version.

SQL / Dapper spans: the API tiers add AddSqlClientInstrumentation(). Dapper executes through Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, so every query/stored-proc call becomes a child DB span (db.system=mssql, db.name, duration, error status) nested under the request + correlated to the rest of the trace — you see exactly which DB calls a request made and how long each took. The SQL statement text is NOT captured by default (avoids logging query text/PII); enable it deliberately with AddSqlClientInstrumentation(o => o.SetDbStatementForText = true) if you want the command text on spans.

The UI tiers (AppManagement's AdminConsole + generated Blazor Servers) are instrumented too, under the same opt-in switch. There the win is HttpClient instrumentation: every call from the UI to the API/Gateway joins the same trace, so a UI action links end-to-end to its API server span and DB. (A Blazor Server's interactive circuit isn't request-per-action, so AspNetCore spans there are sparser than on the API tiers — the HttpClient hop is the useful signal.)

docs.title: Transactional Outbox
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Data · Namespace: Asdamir.Data.Outbox

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The transactional outbox delivers messages (email, SMS) reliably. Instead of calling an SMTP/SMS gateway inline — where a crash or a slow gateway loses the message or blocks the request — you write the message to an outbox table in the same transaction as your business change. A background worker then claims and dispatches it, with retries and dead-lettering.

This gives at-least-once delivery decoupled from the request path.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
enqueue row ──▶ Outbox_ClaimBatch ──▶ IOutboxDispatcher (by MessageType)
                     ▲                         │
                     │                  success │ transient fail │ permanent fail
              reclaim stale locks       MarkDone │ MarkRetry      │ MarkDead
  • Claim: the worker claims a batch (Outbox_ClaimBatch) and stamps a worker lock.
  • Dispatch: each row is routed to the IOutboxDispatcher for its MessageType (1 = SMS, 2 = Email).
  • Outcome: success → MarkDone; transient failure → MarkRetry with exponential backoff + jitter; permanent failure (or attempts exhausted) → MarkDead.
  • Self-healing: locks abandoned by a crashed worker are reclaimed after a stale threshold.

docs.title: Dispatchers
docs.text:
A dispatcher implements IOutboxDispatcher:

public interface IOutboxDispatcher
{
    byte MessageType { get; }                                   // 1 = SMS, 2 = Email
    Task DispatchAsync(ClaimedOutboxMessage message, CancellationToken ct);
}
  • MailDispatcher (MailKit) — multi-To/Cc/Bcc, ReplyTo, per-message From, HTML and attachments. Once the SMTP server has accepted a message, a failure while closing the session is logged and not surfaced as a dispatch failure — the message is sent, and reporting otherwise would make the worker retry it and deliver a duplicate.
  • SmsDispatcher — a stub you replace with your provider; a Twilio dispatcher is provided in the management app.

Throw a PermanentDispatchException to skip retries and dead-letter immediately (e.g. an unparseable address); throw anything else to schedule a retry.

docs.title: Worker options
docs.text:
The worker is bound from Outbox:Worker:

"Outbox": {
  "Worker": {
    "Enabled": true,
    "BatchSize": 25,
    "PollInterval": "00:00:01",
    "IdleBackoff": "00:00:05",
    "BackoffBaseSeconds": 30,
    "BackoffMaxSeconds": 3600,
    "JitterPercent": 0.20,
    "ReclaimStaleThresholdMinutes": 5
  }
}

SMTP transport is configured under Smtp; SMS provider selection under Sms (Stub | Twilio) with credentials under Twilio.

docs.title: Sending mail directly (IEmailService)
docs.text:
IEmailService sends through SMTP inline, without the outbox — prefer the outbox for anything that must not be lost. Two behaviours are worth knowing when you do call it:

  • SendBulkAsync throws BulkEmailSendException when any recipient fails. Every recipient is attempted first; the exception then carries FailedRecipients (retry these, not the whole list — the rest were mailed), TotalRecipients and AllFailed. The addresses are deliberately not part of the exception message, so logging it does not write them to the log. Cancellation propagates as OperationCanceledException, not as a per-recipient failure.
  • As with MailDispatcher, a failure while disconnecting after a successful send is logged, not thrown.

Upgrade note. SendBulkAsync used to complete normally even when sends had failed. Callers that relied on that must now catch BulkEmailSendException (and can retry just FailedRecipients).

docs.title: Fail-closed by design
docs.text: An unconfigured gateway is treated as a permanent failure, not a silent success — the row surfaces in the AdminConsole "Failed" view instead of pretending it was sent.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: Package: Asdamir.Core · Namespace: Asdamir.Core.Validation

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Asdamir layers three complementary validation styles:

  1. FluentValidation validators for request/command objects.
  2. Data-annotation attributes, including framework-specific ones (e.g. phone validation backed by libphonenumber).
  3. A business-rule engine for cross-cutting, runtime-evaluated rules.

docs.title: Registration
docs.text:
builder.Services.AddValidation();                    // core validation services
builder.Services.AddValidationWithFluentValidation(); // + FluentValidation assembly scanning
// or the umbrella:
builder.Services.AddFullValidation();

AddValidationWithFluentValidation registers all AbstractValidator<T> implementations found in your assemblies.

docs.title: FluentValidation
docs.text:
public sealed class CreateUserValidator : AbstractValidator<CreateUserRequest>
{
    public CreateUserValidator()
    {
        RuleFor(x => x.Email).NotEmpty().EmailAddress();
        RuleFor(x => x.Name).NotEmpty().MaximumLength(200);
    }
}

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Use standard System.ComponentModel.DataAnnotations attributes plus the framework's additions:

public sealed record ContactDto(
    [property: Required] string Name,
    [property: Phone] string PhoneNumber);   // Asdamir.Core.Validation.PhoneAttribute (libphonenumber)

The [Phone] attribute validates real, dialable numbers (not just a regex) via libphonenumber.

docs.title: Business-rule engine
docs.text: For rules that depend on runtime state (time windows, tenant policy, cross-entity checks), implement IBusinessRule and evaluate them through the engine. This keeps imperative "can this happen right now?" logic out of your controllers and testable in isolation.
